# Fluid Dispensing Devices for Multi-Compartment Liquid Delivery Systems

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to fluid dispensing devices specifically engineered to dispense two or more distinct liquids from a single container. A primary application of this technology involves the dispensing of bleach and a corresponding bleach activator, which are stored separately within a bottle configured with first and second compartments. By maintaining physical separation between these two reactive components until the point of dispensing, the invention addresses common challenges associated with multi-component liquid delivery systems.

## Delayed Mixing to Minimize Residue

A central objective of the invention is to delay the mixing of the two liquids for as long as possible during the dispensing process. This delayed-mixing approach serves to minimize the presence of mixed composition residue that would otherwise remain within the internal pathways of the dispensing device between uses. When two reactive liquids, such as bleach and its activator, are allowed to combine and then sit stagnant within tubing or pump mechanisms, the resulting mixture can degrade in efficacy over time or create undesirable buildup. By engineering the device to keep the liquids separate until the last possible moment—ideally at or near the point of dispensing—the invention helps preserve the potency and performance characteristics of the final combined product delivered to the user.

## Dual Dip Tube and Pump Configurations

To achieve this separation, certain embodiments of the invention employ separate dip tubes, each dedicated to drawing liquid from its respective compartment within the bottle. Each dip tube is paired with its own independent pump mechanism, allowing the two liquids to be drawn simultaneously and independently from their respective storage areas. This dual-tube, dual-pump architecture ensures that the bleach and bleach activator remain isolated from one another throughout the majority of their journey from the compartments to the dispensing outlet, with mixing occurring only at the final stage of dispensing, such as at a shared nozzle or mixing chamber.

## Single Tube and Pump Alternatives

While dual dip tube and dual pump configurations offer maximum separation, the invention also contemplates simplified embodiments in which a single delivery tube or a single pump is used to service both compartments. These streamlined configurations are suitable in circumstances where the resulting volume of mixed composition that may reside within the shared components remains sufficiently small so as not to compromise the desired efficacy of the dispensed product. In such cases, the reduced complexity and cost of a single-tube or single-pump system can be advantageous, provided that the small residual mixture does not adversely affect performance or shelf life between uses.

## Advantages of Dual Delivery Tube Configurations

One of the notable benefits of configurations employing dual delivery tubes is the elimination of the need to prime the device prior to use. In single-tube systems, residual mixed composition from a previous dispensing cycle may remain within the shared tubing, necessitating an initial "priming" spray to clear out this old, potentially degraded mixture before fresh, properly proportioned liquid can be dispensed. Dual delivery tube configurations, by contrast, avoid this issue altogether, since each liquid travels through its own dedicated pathway until the point of final mixing. This design consideration enhances user convenience and ensures more consistent product delivery from the very first actuation of the dispensing device.

# Dual-Compartment Fluid Dispensing Device for Delayed Mixing of Reactive Liquid Components

## Background and Field of the Invention

Many consumer and industrial products are formulated from two or more separate liquid components that must remain isolated from one another until the moment of use. This is particularly true for chemically reactive systems, such as bleach and bleach activator formulations, where premature mixing can lead to degradation of the active ingredients, loss of efficacy, or the formation of unwanted byproducts. Conventional dispensing systems that store pre-mixed formulations suffer from a limited shelf life, as the combined chemistry begins to degrade immediately upon mixing, often well before the product is fully consumed by the end user.

Furthermore, in traditional dual-liquid dispensing systems where components are combined internally within a shared delivery pathway, there is often a substantial volume of mixed product residing within the device's internal tubing, nozzle, or dispensing head at any given time. When the device is not used for an extended period, this residual mixed composition can degrade, resulting in a diminished quality of product upon the next use. To counteract this issue, users are frequently required to "prime" the device by actuating it multiple times to purge the degraded mixture before fresh, effective product can be dispensed. This priming step is not only wasteful of the product but also inconvenient for the user and can lead to inconsistent performance if the priming step is neglected or improperly performed.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention addresses these shortcomings by providing a fluid dispensing device configured to store and dispense two distinct liquid components from a dual-compartment bottle, while delaying the mixing of these components until the precise moment of dispensing. The device utilizes a bottle having two separate internal compartments, each containing a different liquid formulation—for example, a bleach solution in one compartment and a bleach activator in the other. Rather than relying on a shared internal pathway that would allow the two liquids to combine and reside together within the device, the invention employs separate dip tubes extending into each compartment, each dip tube being dedicated to a single liquid component.

Each dip tube is connected to its own corresponding pump mechanism, such that each liquid component has an independent flow path from its compartment through its designated pump. This dual-pump, dual-dip-tube configuration ensures that each liquid remains segregated throughout the majority of its journey through the device, only converging with the other component at or very near the point of final dispensing, such as at a shared or closely positioned nozzle or outlet.

## Detailed Description of Preferred Embodiments

In one exemplary embodiment, the dispensing device comprises a bottle body divided into two separate compartments by an internal partition or through the use of two distinct containers held within a common housing. A first dip tube extends into the first compartment containing, for example, a bleach solution, while a second dip tube extends into the second compartment containing a bleach activator or other reactive additive. Each dip tube terminates at its own dedicated pump, which may be actuated simultaneously through a shared actuator mechanism, such as a single trigger or pump head, or through independently timed actuation mechanisms depending on the desired application.

Upon actuation of the dispensing mechanism, each pump draws its respective liquid component up through its corresponding dip tube. The two liquid streams travel through separate internal channels within the device, remaining isolated from one another throughout most of the internal flow path. The two streams are only permitted to converge and mix at the final dispensing point, such as at an outlet nozzle, spray head, or discharge orifice, where they combine into a unified spray or stream that is delivered to the target surface or substrate.

This configuration—wherein each liquid component travels through a substantially isolated pathway comprising its own dip tube and pump—provides several notable advantages over conventional dual-liquid dispensing systems. First, the amount of mixed composition residing within the device at any given time is minimized, as the two components are not combined until the very last moment of dispensing. This significantly reduces the risk of degradation of the mixed product between uses, as there is little to no pre-mixed formulation sitting stagnant within the internal tubing or nozzle assembly of the device.

Second, because there is minimal residual mixed product within the device, the invention can largely eliminate the need for users to prime the device prior to use. In conventional systems, users are often required to actuate the pump several times to expel old, degraded product that has been sitting within the mixing chamber or shared delivery tube since the last use. With the present invention's dual delivery tube configuration, however, each actuation draws fresh, unmixed product from each compartment, such that the liquids only combine at the point of dispensing, ensuring that the user consistently receives a freshly mixed, fully effective product with each use.

## Alternative Embodiments

While the primary embodiment describes a bleach and bleach activator system, it will be understood by those skilled in the art that the principles of this invention may be readily applied to any number of multi-component liquid systems where separation of components prior to dispensing is desirable. This may include, but is not limited to, two-part epoxies, reactive cleaning formulations, cosmetic products with unstable active ingredients, or any other combination of liquids that benefit from delayed mixing.

Additionally, while the preferred embodiment describes the use of two dip tubes and two corresponding pumps, alternative configurations may incorporate additional dip tubes and pumps to accommodate three or more separate liquid components, each remaining isolated until the point of dispensing. The actuation mechanism for the pumps may be a single combined actuator that operates both pumps simultaneously through a shared trigger, lever, or button, or alternatively, separate actuators may be provided for each pump to allow for independent or sequential dispensing of each component, depending on the desired application and formulation requirements.

## Advantages of the Invention

The dispensing device described herein offers numerous advantages over existing dual-liquid dispensing systems. By maintaining separate flow paths for each liquid component through dedicated dip tubes and pumps, the invention substantially reduces the volume of mixed product that may degrade within the device between uses. This not only improves the overall performance and effectiveness of the dispensed product but also enhances user convenience by reducing or eliminating the need for priming prior to use. Additionally, the modular nature of the dual dip tube and pump configuration allows for versatile application across a wide range of multi-component liquid products, making this invention broadly applicable to numerous industries and use cases where the delayed mixing of reactive or unstable liquid formulations is desired.

# The Value of Individual Perspective

Each person carries within them a unique collection of experiences, memories, and ways of seeing the world. The tendency to group people into broad categories—by nationality, profession, or belief—can sometimes obscure this fundamental truth: no two individuals are truly alike.

The importance of recognizing this becomes clear when we consider how easily we fall into patterns of generalization. We might say "the young generation thinks this way" or "the older generation believes that," but such statements, while sometimes useful as rough approximations, fail to capture the rich diversity that exists within any group. Each member of a community, family, or profession brings something distinct to the table.

To separate the individual from the collective is not to deny the value of community or shared identity—these connections matter deeply and shape who we are. Rather, it means taking care not to lose sight of the person within the crowd. The colleague who seems to represent "management" is still someone with private hopes and struggles. The stranger who fits a stereotype is still someone whose story remains untold until we take the time to listen.

The challenge, then, is to hold two truths simultaneously: that we are shaped by our shared contexts, and that each of us remains irreducibly our own. When we separate these threads carefully, we begin to see people not as representatives of a category, but as the complex, individual beings they truly are.

In practice, this means pausing before we judge, asking questions before we assume, and remembering that behind every generalization stands a person who cannot be fully captured by it. The effort to see each person clearly, apart from the labels we might apply, is perhaps one of the most quietly radical acts of respect we can offer one another.

# BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to dispensing containers for storing and dispensing chemically reactive substances, and more particularly to a dual-compartment bottle dispenser configured to maintain bleach and a bleach activator compound in physically isolated storage compartments until the moment of dispensing, at which point the two components are combined to form an activated cleaning or disinfecting solution.

## Description of the Related Art

Bleach, typically formulated as an aqueous solution of sodium hypochlorite, is widely used as a disinfecting and whitening agent in household, industrial, and institutional settings. While effective on its own, the cleaning, disinfecting, and stain-removal performance of bleach can be substantially enhanced through the addition of an activator compound. Bleach activators, such as tetraacetylethylenediamine (TAED) or various peroxide-based compounds, react with bleach to generate more reactive oxidizing species, thereby improving cleaning efficacy, reducing required contact times, and enabling effective performance at lower temperatures.

A significant obstacle to commercializing combined bleach-and-activator products, however, is the chemical instability that results when these two components are stored together over extended periods. Bleach activators tend to react with sodium hypochlorite even under ambient storage conditions, gradually consuming the activator and degrading the bleach before the product ever reaches the point of use. This premature reaction diminishes the effectiveness of the final product, shortens shelf life, and can generate unwanted byproducts, gas evolution, or pressure buildup within a sealed container. Manufacturers have therefore been largely unable to offer a stable, pre-mixed bleach-and-activator product with a commercially viable shelf life.

To address this instability, various packaging approaches have been proposed for storing reactive two-part formulations separately and combining them only at the time of use. Known solutions include separate bottles or packets requiring the user to manually measure and mix each component, dual-chamber containers with frangible seals or valves that must be manually ruptured or actuated, and multi-compartment pouches dispensed through separate spouts. While these approaches achieve some degree of separation between reactive components, they present a number of practical drawbacks.

Many existing dual-compartment designs require the user to perform an additional manual step—such as breaking a seal, twisting a valve, or squeezing a separate chamber—before or during dispensing, which adds complexity and creates opportunities for user error, incomplete mixing, or accidental premature combination of the components during shipping, handling, or storage. Other designs rely on complex internal architectures, multiple moving parts, or specialized closures that increase manufacturing cost and complexity, and that may be prone to leakage or failure at the seal between compartments, particularly under the pressure, temperature fluctuations, and physical handling encountered during shipping and retail distribution.

Additionally, many conventional multi-chamber containers are not well suited to standard high-volume bottling and filling equipment, requiring specialized production lines or modified filling processes that increase manufacturing cost. Others fail to provide a consistent, repeatable, and accurately proportioned mixing ratio between the bleach and activator components at each dispensing event, resulting in inconsistent product performance from use to use.

There remains a need for a bottle dispenser that reliably isolates bleach from a bleach activator throughout storage and transport, that combines the two components automatically and in a consistent ratio at the moment of dispensing without requiring a separate manual mixing step, and that can be manufactured using conventional bottle-forming and filling equipment at a cost suitable for mass-market consumer products. The present invention addresses these needs.

# Dual-Liquid Dispenser: Pump and Tube Configuration Embodiments

In accordance with various embodiments of the present disclosure, the dual-liquid dispenser may be configured with either a single dispensing pathway or with separate, independently actuated pathways for each of the two liquid components, and the selection between these configurations gives rise to distinct advantages and tradeoffs with respect to priming behavior and residual mixed composition retained within the device. In a first embodiment, a single pump and single delivery tube are employed downstream of a mixing junction, wherein the two liquid components are combined at or near the point of pump intake, such that a single actuation stroke draws both components through a common flow path and expels the resulting mixture through a shared nozzle or outlet. This configuration advantageously reduces the number of moving parts and simplifies the overall mechanical assembly, thereby lowering manufacturing complexity and cost; however, it necessarily results in a volume of pre-mixed composition being retained within the shared tube and pump chamber between dispensing events. This residual mixed volume may, in certain embodiments, be subject to chemical instability, phase separation, or degradation over time, particularly where the two liquid components are reactive, incompatible when combined for extended durations, or intended to be combined only immediately prior to use. In an alternative embodiment, the dispenser instead comprises two discrete pumps, each fluidly coupled to a separate delivery tube extending from a respective reservoir containing one of the two liquid components, wherein the two independent flow paths converge only at or immediately adjacent to the dispensing outlet, such as within a mixing nozzle, external mixing chamber, or at the point of egress from the device. This dual-pathway configuration substantially eliminates the retention of pre-mixed composition within the internal tubing, as each component remains isolated until the moment of dispensing, thereby extending the effective shelf life of the individually stored components and reducing the risk of clogging, degradation, or unwanted reactions occurring within the device during periods of non-use. It will further be appreciated that the separate-pathway embodiment may require an initial priming sequence for each individual pump and tube prior to first use or after extended storage, in order to ensure that both components are simultaneously present at the mixing point in the correct ratio upon actuation, whereas the single-pathway embodiment, once initially primed, maintains the mixture ratio inherently by virtue of the shared flow path, at the cost of the aforementioned residual mixture concerns. Accordingly, the choice between a single shared pump/tube configuration and a dual independent pump/tube configuration may be selected based on the chemical compatibility of the components, the desired shelf life, the acceptable priming complexity, and the intended dispensing frequency, and it is contemplated that certain embodiments may further incorporate check valves, purge cycles, or automatic priming routines to mitigate the respective disadvantages of either configuration.
